title: The rebel verbs
goal: Master eight irregular verbs that are among the most frequently used — in both the present and the past.

notes: **Mentem, not menttem.** *Megy* changes completely in the past: its stem becomes *men-*. In the same way *jön* becomes *jöt-*, *eszik* becomes *et-*, *iszik* becomes *it-*. The good news: once the stem has changed, the person endings are the usual ones.

**Evett and ivott are the two forms that surprise people most.** The *ő* form of *eszik* is not *ett* but **evett**, and of *iszik* not *itt* but **ivott**. There is a historical reason, but for now just memorize them — you'll use these two words every day.

**Itt has two completely different meanings.** *Itt* means "here", and *ittak* means "they drank". The context always separates them, but beginners often freeze for a second the first time they meet this.

**Lettem means "I became".** *Lesz* does two jobs: the future of *van* (unit 8), and "become" (*Fáradt lettem* = I got tired, *Orvos lett* = he became a doctor). English keeps "will be" and "become" apart; Hungarian uses one word.

**Haza, itthon, otthon.** Three words that all relate to home but can't be swapped. *Haza* means "(to) home" (direction), *itthon* means "at home" when you're there right now, and *otthon* means "at home" when you aren't. English doesn't tell the last two apart at all.

grammars.title: Eight irregular verbs — present
body: All of them are used very often, and precisely for that reason the language has never tidied up their forms.
after: Note *mész* in the *megy* row — the only *te* form in the whole list that truly can't be guessed. The rest still follow the pattern you know, just with a changed stem.
*Visz* (to carry, take away) and *hisz* (to believe) follow *tesz* and *vesz* exactly: *viszek, viszel, visz…* and *hiszek, hiszel, hisz…*

grammars.title: Eight irregular verbs — past
body: The stem changes, the endings stay as usual.
after: **The definite form just swaps the tail**, as with regular verbs: *ettem, etted, ette, ettük, ettétek, ették*; *ittam, ittad, itta, ittuk, ittátok, itták*; *vettem, vetted, vette, vettük, vettétek, vették*.
*Lesz* in the past becomes *lettem, lettél, lett, lettünk, lettetek, lettek* — and its meaning shifts to "became", not "will be": *Orvos lett* = he became a doctor.

*Ez az otthonom.* = This is my home.

after: The same split applies to countries: *itthon* if you're in Hungary and talking about Hungary, *otthon* if you're abroad and missing it. This subtlety never makes your sentence misunderstood, but using it correctly instantly sounds like someone who really lives there.
Its siblings for other places: *ide* (to here), *oda* (to there), *itt* (here), *ott* (there), *innen* (from here), *onnan* (from there).

blocks.text: Three day trips from Budapest that locals mention most: **Szentendre** (an artists' town on the Danube, forty minutes by boat), **Esztergom** (Hungary's biggest basilica), and **a Balaton** — the largest lake in Central Europe, which Hungarians call "the Hungarian sea" without a hint of joking.

blocks.title: Ten verbs that cover most stories
items: If you only have time to memorize ten past forms, pick these: *voltam, mentem, jöttem, ettem, ittam, láttam, csináltam, olvastam, néztem, aludtam*.
Together the ten cover more than half of the past-tense sentences in everyday conversation — and six of them are irregular, so they really have to come from memory, not from rules.
